plain_summary: The Engle Lab invents new chemical reactions that build complex molecules faster and more precisely. Most of their work uses metal catalysts, especially palladium, nickel, and copper, to speed up reactions and control exactly which product forms, down to its 3D shape. A signature strategy is attaching a small "directing group" to a starting molecule that grabs the metal and steers the reaction to a specific spot, enabling additions across double and triple bonds, formation of strained rings, and creation of hard-to-make carbon centers. The lab also designs new catalyst precursors that are stable in air, making them easier and safer to use. More recently, they have branched into chemical biology, using high-throughput chemistry to discover small molecules that force two proteins together, a strategy used in modern drug design. This matters because more selective reactions using cheaper, more available metals make it faster and less costly to build medicines and new materials.
trajectory: Recent papers show the lab pushing deeper into mechanistically guided ligand design, tuning the flexibility of directing auxiliaries and the redox behavior of quinone ligands to unlock reactions and reaction rates that were previously inaccessible, alongside continued development of air-stable, earth-abundant nickel and copper catalyst precursors. The lab is also expanding into chemical biology, applying its high-throughput chemistry expertise to discover chemical inducers of proximity for targeted protein degradation, suggesting a growing bridge between synthetic methodology and drug discovery.
